title: US and Saudi Arabia Launch First Joint Strikes on Iran-Backed Militias in Iraq, Killing at Least 20
excerpt: The unprecedented operation targeted weapons and logistics sites across eastern Iraq after more than 30 drone attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure in 72 hours.
body:
• US and Saudi fighter jets struck multiple weapons and logistics sites across eastern Iraq in the first confirmed joint military operation against Iran-backed militias.
  • Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces reported at least 20 fighters killed and 32 wounded in the overnight strikes.
  • The operation followed more than 30 IRGC-directed drone attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure in 72 hours, including strikes that shut down a refinery producing 400,000 barrels per day.
  • Brent crude surged 3.1% to $84.58 per barrel as markets priced in further escalation across the region.

A New Front in the West Asia Conflict

US Central Command and the Saudi Arabian Armed Forces launched precision strikes across eastern Iraq on Tuesday, targeting what they described as Iran-aligned terrorist logistics and weapons sites. The operation marks a sharp escalation in the broader West Asia conflict — the first time Saudi Arabia has publicly confirmed striking targets inside Iraq and the first joint US-Saudi combat operation in the country.

https://x.com/AJEnglish/status/2082387674845843587

"U.S. and Saudi fighter aircraft struck multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq in a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours," CENTCOM said in a statement, adding that the attacks on Saudi infrastructure were "unwarranted."

Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), a coalition of primarily Shiite, Iran-backed armed groups that is officially part of Iraq's military, said at least 20 of its fighters were killed and 32 others wounded. The PMF said several of its official headquarters across different parts of Iraq were hit.

"The Kingdom emphasizes that it does not seek escalation but will respond to any aggression it faces."

— Saudi Defense Ministry statement

Iran's Ballistic Missile Salvo

The joint strikes came hours after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired ballistic missiles at the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, which houses US forces, and at the headquarters of US Central Command in the region. Jordan's military said it intercepted and destroyed five Iranian missiles, with no immediate reports of casualties.

The missile attack followed nearly two weeks of daily US bombings that primarily targeted Iran's ability to threaten shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has countered with several retaliatory strikes against Gulf states, sometimes hitting near US bases.

Since July 7, some 225 US service members have been injured in the conflict. Four American troops have been killed — three at the Jordan base on July 17 and one at Erbil Air Base in Iraq two days later during a controlled detonation of a downed Iranian drone.

Iraq Caught in the Crossfire

Iraqi President Nizar Amidi condemned the US-Saudi airstrikes as "an unacceptable attack and a blatant violation of Iraq's sovereignty, targeting its official security institutions." He also said Iraq should not be a "launching pad or arena for attacks against neighboring countries or for settling regional and international scores."

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi cancelled a planned visit to Riyadh and convened an emergency National Security Council meeting. Analysts say Saudi Arabia chose to send a blunt message by going public and going big with the strikes, rather than continuing its earlier pattern of covert operations.

"It's a very sensitive time and they want to deter the Iraqis as much as possible," said a source familiar with Saudi government thinking, according to The Times. The strikes were conducted jointly with the US to "go bigger" than previous Saudi operations.

Oil Markets React

Brent crude jumped 3.1% to $84.58 per barrel on Wednesday as traders weighed the risk of further escalation. Saudi Arabia has faced sustained attacks on its energy infrastructure from two directions — Iranian-backed militias in Iraq to its northeast and Houthi forces in Yemen to its south. Earlier this week, drone strikes forced the shutdown of a refinery at Jizan producing 400,000 barrels per day.

In a diplomatic move, Oman has presented Iran with a plan backed by Gulf states to jointly manage the Strait of Hormuz, including voluntary fees from passing ships. Under the proposal, Iran would not exercise sole control of the chokepoint.

What It Means for Indians in the Gulf

The escalation raises fresh concerns for the estimated 8.5 million Indians living and working across the Gulf states, the largest diaspora population in the region. Rising oil prices also threaten India's import bill — the country imports over 85% of its crude oil, with a significant share sourced from Gulf producers. The Indian Embassy in Iraq has previously urged citizens to exercise caution and keep travel documents ready.
nri_angle: Millions of Indians working in Gulf states face heightened security risks as the conflict escalates, while rising oil prices threaten India's import bill.
